title: The Platform

post.author: u/night_visits_ciarnait
post.title: I pressed "check in" once at a diabetic cat's home. The app logged me arriving four times in six seconds, then cancelled his next three visits as done.

blocks.text: I'm Ciarnait, a night sitter for Moonmitten, an agency that visits pets at home while their owners are away. At each visit I press "check in" on the agency's app, so the owner knows I came.
The app runs on 40 small programs, each with one job. One program asking another to do something and answer is a call. Each of these programs is a service. Five teams build them.

Every service starts from the same ready-made kit, kept by a sixth team. The kit is the platform. The starting copy each new service is made from is the template. Change the template and every service changes.

The template puts a small helper beside each service to carry its calls. That helper is a sidecar. A call goes through it in steps: it receives the call, sends it on, then waits up to a set time, the limit per try. If no answer comes, it cuts the try.

Then it may send the same call again: a retry. Version 2 of the platform never retried. Version 3, put into all 40 services at once on Tuesday 3 November, gives every call a 2-second limit per try and up to 3 retries.
Tobermory is a diabetic cat. His owner is away, and his vet wants him seen every two hours. Tonight's plan held four visits: 02:00, 04:00, 06:00 and 08:00, the 06:00 one with his insulin.

A call that only looks something up, like loading my route, is a read. A call that saves something is a write. A check-in is a write, done by the visit service, which keeps every booking, in two steps: it saves a check-in line, then marks the home's earliest visit not yet done as done.

Wednesday 4 November, 02:13:07. One press. The phone spun for eight seconds, then said "Check-in failed. Please try again." Our handbook says press once, never twice. I rang the night line, which rings the engineer on call.
At 02:14:00 my phone buzzed: "Tobermory: next visits cancelled: done."

The text came from the rota service, which plans our routes. Once a minute, on the minute, it checks every route and texts any change. On the booking screen, my next three visits there said "cancelled: done", the 06:00 insulin visit too.

Eoghan, the visits team's engineer on call, rang back and read me the visit service's log. Each line shows the moment a call reached the service, not when its save finished, then the home and what was saved:

02:13:07  Tobermory  check-in saved  02:00 visit done
02:13:09  Tobermory  check-in saved  04:00 visit done
02:13:11  Tobermory  check-in saved  06:00 visit done
02:13:13  Tobermory  check-in saved  08:00 visit done

Every night from 02:00 to 02:30 a report reads the day's visits, and the visit service slows from 0.4 seconds an answer to 2.5. Every try was cut at 2 seconds, and the sidecar retried three times, but each carried on and saved a check-in half a second later. Mine was the only visit in that half hour: the first check-in during the report since version 3.

blocks.label: tobermory_0213.png

diagram.aria: Wednesday 4 November 2026, 02:13:05 to 02:13:20. One press at 02:13:07. Try 1 reaches the visit service at 02:13:07, the sidecar waits 2 seconds and cuts it at 02:13:09, and the visit service carries on and saves a check-in at 02:13:09.5. Try 2 runs 02:13:09 to a cut at 02:13:11 and saves at 02:13:11.5; try 3, 02:13:11, cut at 02:13:13, saved at 02:13:13.5; try 4, 02:13:13, cut at 02:13:15, saved at 02:13:15.5. The app waits from 02:13:07 and says check-in failed at 02:13:15.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Eoghan's reading of the log, Wednesday 4 November 2026. Amber: the sidecar waiting, up to 2 seconds a try. Red: the visit service still working after the cut. The log stamps each try with the moment it arrived, 02:13:07, :09, :11 and :13; each save landed 2.5 seconds after its try began, at :09.5, :11.5, :13.5 and :15.5. The pause between tries is a few hundredths of a second, too small to show. Save 1 marked the 02:00 visit done; saves 2, 3 and 4 marked the 04:00, 06:00 and 08:00 visits done before I reached them. The app gave up at 02:13:15, eight seconds after the press.

blocks.text: Nothing I touched went wrong: one press, one phone, one cat asleep on the radiator. The setting that did it was chosen in a building I've never been in. What should Moonmitten change before tomorrow night?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Two questions. Which of your calls are safe to repeat, meaning a second copy changes nothing? Loading your route is one. Is a check-in? And when try 2 reached the visit service, could it tell it had seen this check-in before? In The Ticket Number, the box office gave each sale a key: a name made once for the job and sent with every try, so a repeat could be spotted. What does a Moonmitten check-in carry?

replies.author: u/night_visits_ciarnait
replies.text: Eoghan says a check-in carries the home and the time, nothing else, so every try looked new. Loading my route changes nothing however often it runs. A check-in marks one more visit done each time it lands. Four landed: 02:13:09.5, 11.5, 13.5 and 15.5.

comments.author: u/retries_are_free_sigeberht
comments.text: Retries are free resilience: the knack of carrying on when a call goes missing. Networks, the links between machines, drop calls all the time; a sidecar that tries again is why your app works at all. The bug is the 2-second limit. It's far too tight for a slow night. Make it 10 and every try finishes before it's cut.

comments.author: u/own_your_settings_gisilberta
comments.text: This is what happens when one team decides for forty services. The visits team knows its service crawls at 02:00; the platform team in another office doesn't. Let each team set its own retries and limits, and stop inheriting someone else's guess.

replies.author: u/night_visits_ciarnait
replies.text: Eoghan said the visits team heard about version 3 when it arrived, along with the other 39 services.

reply.prompt: Tobermory's owner is away until Friday, so tomorrow night holds the same four visits, and the report runs at 02:00 as always. What should Moonmitten change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Raise the platform's limit per try from 2 seconds to 10, so that slow calls can finish.
options.part2: That Wednesday afternoon the platform team raised the limit per try to 10 seconds for all 40 services. In the sim, set the limit to 10: at 2.5 seconds the first try finishes, one check-in, and every visit stays booked. For four weeks nothing happened. Through November the agency took on more homes and the report grew. In the sim, make the slow answer 12 seconds and play: tries reach the visit service at 02:13:07, :17, :27 and :37, each is cut at 10 seconds, and each saves 12 seconds after it began, at :19, :29, :39 and :49. That is what happened on Wednesday 2 December 2026, Tobermory's owner away again: four check-ins, the 04:00, 06:00 and 08:00 visits cancelled as done, and the rota service's text at 02:14:00.
options.senior: A longer limit only moves the line the slow answer has to cross. The real problem is that the sidecar retried a write: a cut try is not a failed try, only one whose answer nobody waited for, and the visit service kept working and saved it. Any limit shorter than the slowest answer, on any night, turns one press into several check-ins. A limit per try is worth setting from each service's measured slow answer rather than one guess for all 40, but it can't make a write safe to repeat; only the service recognising a repeat can.

options.text: Move the nightly report to 04:00, so the visit service is fast when sitters check in.
options.part2: That Wednesday afternoon the report was moved to 04:00 to 04:30, from the next night on. In the sim, set the report to 04:00 and play: the 02:13:07 press answers in 0.4 seconds, one check-in. That is how Thursday 5 November began. At the 04:00 visit I pressed at 04:13:07, inside the report: four tries, check-ins saved at 04:13:09.5, 11.5, 13.5 and 15.5. The first marked the 04:00 visit done, the next two cancelled the 06:00 insulin visit and the 08:00, and the fourth found no visit left. The rota service texted me at 04:14:00.
options.senior: Moving the report moves the hour at which the visit service is slow, and sitters work all night, so it only moves whose check-in doubles. The cause is a rule in the platform, retry every call, meeting a write that does something each time it lands. Any slow moment, a report, a busy hour, a struggling database, will meet that rule again. Scheduling heavy work for quiet hours is good practice, but it is capacity planning, not a fix for repeated writes.

options.text: Retry only calls marked safe to repeat; each write carries a key the service checks.
options.part2: That Wednesday morning Mirjam, who leads the platform team, put the visit service back on version 2 while they changed the template. The new rule became an API standard every template enforces: a call is retried only if it is marked safe to repeat, and every write carries a key the service checks. The app makes the key from the visit's number, 8841 for Tobermory's 02:00 visit, before the first try. On Tuesday 10 November the change went to 3 services first, photos, search and messages, their owners told; on Tuesday 17 November to the other 37, each team told what would change. In the sim, retry only safe calls and turn on the key check: one try at 02:13:07, cut at 02:13:09, saved at 02:13:09.5. The app still said "Check-in failed": during the report no answer comes inside 2 seconds, and the visits team, told this time, is working on it. The handbook now says press again if it fails. Turn on the second press: at 02:13:14 the key check refuses it. That is what happened at 02:13 on Wednesday 18 November, Tobermory's owner away again: one check-in, and the 06:00 insulin visit stayed booked.
options.senior: Two rules, kept by the platform for every team. Retry only what is safe to repeat: reads, and writes the service can recognise. And make writes recognisable: the caller names the job once, with a key, before the first try, and the service looks the key up as each try arrives, does the work for a new key and refuses one it has seen. Then a cut try, a retry or a worried second press all come to one check-in. The platform is the right place for both, because a default there reaches all 40 services at once, which is also why its changes go to a few services first, with their owners told and watching.

options.text: Let each of the 5 teams set its own retries and time limits instead of the template's.
options.verdict: Trade-off: no shared mistake, no shared path
options.part2: That Wednesday afternoon the platform team handed each team its own retries and limits. In the sim, switch on team-owned settings: the visits team chose no retries and a 5-second limit, so one try, one check-in, and every visit stayed booked. By December the 40 services had settings copied from wherever their team last looked. The photos team copied the visits team and turned retries off, though a dropped upload from a sitter's phone in a basement is exactly what a retry is for, and photos stopped arriving. In January the platform team wanted every write to carry a key, and had to ask five teams to change 40 services by hand.
options.senior: Team-owned settings remove the shared surprise: no default changes under you on a Tuesday afternoon. The price is that 40 services must each get retries, limits and keys right, mostly by copying, and the easy, supported way, the golden path, is gone. A platform team's job is to make the right thing the default, not to hand every team the knobs. The better balance is a safe default in the template, a way for owners to change it with a reason written down, and changes to the default rolled out a few services at a time.

sim.title: Replay Tobermory's night, 4 November 2026
sim.lede: You're Ciarnait, replaying the night of Tuesday 3 November 2026 a visit at a time. As given data: Tobermory's plan holds four visits, 02:00, 04:00, 06:00 and 08:00, numbered 8841 to 8844, and at each one you press check in at 13 minutes 7 seconds past the hour. Each press is a write to the visit service, carried by the sidecar. The visit service answers in 0.4 seconds, or 2.5 seconds during the nightly report, 02:00 to 02:30; during the report every answer is slow, a refusal too. A 12-second answer stands for a bigger report. Version 3 of the platform gives every call a 2-second limit per try and up to 3 retries; version 2 had no limit and no retries. The pause between tries, a few hundredths of a second, counts as nothing here. A cut try is not stopped: the visit service finishes it and saves a check-in, and each check-in marks the earliest visit still booked as done. The rota service checks every route once a minute, on the minute, and texts any change. With the key check on, the key is the visit's number: the visit service looks it up as each try arrives, does the work for a new key and refuses one it has already noted. If you press again after an error, it is 5 seconds after the app says the check-in failed. Given data for the other settings: with team-owned settings, the visits team picks no retries and a 5-second limit; with a few first, version 3 goes to 3 services, photos, search and messages, their owners told, and the visit service waits for the next week.
sim.tryThis: Try this: play the night as built: tries reach the visit service at 02:13:07, :09, :11 and :13, save at :09.5, :11.5, :13.5 and :15.5, and the 04:00, 06:00 and 08:00 visits are cancelled; one text at 02:14:00. Set the platform to version 2: one check-in. Turn on the key check: four tries, one check-in, three refused. Retry only calls marked safe to repeat: one try; then turn on the second press and watch it cancel the 04:00 visit, until the key check catches it. Move the report to 04:00: the doubles move to the 04:00 visit. Set the limit to 10, then make the slow answer 12 seconds. Try team-owned settings, and version 3 to a few first.

explain.oneLine: Nobody pressed twice. The platform's version 3 told every sidecar to cut a try after 2 seconds and retry up to 3 times, writes included; during the nightly report the visit service took 2.5 seconds, so each try was cut and retried while the visit service went on and saved it. Four check-ins marked all four of tonight's visits done, and the rota service cancelled the three she hadn't made.

steps.title: A call through the sidecar, step by step.
steps.text: The app's service doesn't call the visit service directly; its sidecar does. All the sidecars and their settings together are called a service mesh. First the sidecar receives the call. Next it finds where the visit service is running, the job The Front Desk gave a registry, and sends the call on. Then it waits, up to the limit per try: 2 seconds in version 3. If no answer comes, it cuts the try, and here is what can go wrong: cutting only stops the waiting. The visit service never hears about the cut and finishes the work. Last, the sidecar retries, up to 3 times, a few hundredths of a second later. Version 3 did this for every call, reads and writes alike. Outside the report the visit service answers in 0.4 seconds, so no try was ever cut and the retries never ran. Version 2 had neither a limit nor retries, so before Tuesday a slow answer was just slow.

steps.title: Why four check-ins: a write that wasn't safe to repeat.
steps.text: A read, such as loading the route, changes nothing, so a second copy is harmless: it is safe to repeat. A check-in is a write in two steps: save a check-in line, then mark the home's earliest visit not yet done as done. It names the home, not the visit, so each copy that lands does real work. At 02:13:07 try 1 arrived and was cut at :09; it saved at :09.5 and marked the 02:00 visit done. Try 2 arrived at :09, nothing told the visit service it was a repeat, and at :11.5 it marked the 04:00 visit done. Tries 3 and 4 took the 06:00 and 08:00. The log stamps each line with the moment a try arrived, which is why the four times sit exactly 2 seconds apart. Once a minute the rota service saw three visits done before she reached them, took them off her route and texted her. Pressing once, as the handbook says, could not help: she did.

steps.title: The platform: one default, 40 services at once.
steps.text: An internal developer platform is the kit a company's own teams build on: here the template, the sidecar and its settings, kept by one team for five others. Done well it is run as a product, with the teams as its customers, and it offers a golden path: the easy, supported way to build a service, so most teams never have to think about retries. That is its strength and tonight's danger: a default set in the template reaches every service on the day it changes. Istio, a widely used service mesh, retries an HTTP call twice by default and sets no timeout at all, so the 3 retries and the 2-second limit were Moonmitten's platform team's own choice; Istio's own documentation shows the same numbers as an example. Version 3 went to all 40 services on Tuesday afternoon, and its first test against a slow write was a cat's check-in at 02:13.

steps.title: The fix as an API standard, rolled out a few at a time.
steps.text: Rule 3, from The Ticket Number: "If the register asks you to charge a customer again, check the ticket number first." The platform makes it a standard every template enforces. First, calls are marked: reads safe to repeat, writes not, unless they carry a key. Second, a key in steps: the app names the job once, before the first try, from the visit's number, 8841; the visit service looks the key up as each try arrives; a new key is noted as in progress and the work done; a key already noted is refused, with the first result. What can go wrong: a key made per press, not per visit, misses her second press, and a key forgotten too soon lets a late repeat through. Third, a platform change goes to a few services first, their owners told what changes and what to watch, then wider, as Canary in the Mine did with servers. A longer limit, a moved report or team-owned settings each fix one night and leave the write unsafe or the path broken.

steps.title: The walk into the platform team's building.
steps.text: Everything Ciarnait could touch was fine: one press, one phone, an app that showed exactly what it was told, a cat asleep on the radiator. The cause was a line written on a Tuesday afternoon by people she had never met, in an office in another town. On Friday she took the train there, because Mirjam asked her to tell the platform team what a cancelled visit looks like from a kitchen at 02:14. Their room was quiet, six desks and a whiteboard of version numbers. On one screen sat the template, open at version 3: two settings, a limit of 2 seconds and 3 retries, with no word anywhere about which calls they would land on.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for tomorrow night. The app's service sends the check-in with key 8841 to its sidecar. The sidecar sends a write as one try and retries only reads. The visit service keeps a key list and refuses a key it has already noted. Below: the template, which now retries only calls marked safe to repeat, feeds the sidecar; template changes roll out to a few services first, their owners told, before the visit service.

nodes.label: Rollout: a few first, owners told

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for tomorrow night. The app names the job with key 8841 before the first try. The sidecar sends a write once and retries only calls marked safe to repeat. The visit service notes each key as a try arrives and refuses one it has seen, so a retry or a second press can't save a second check-in. Template changes reach a few services first, their owners told, before the other 37. In the sim: one check-in at 02:13:09.5, and a second press at 02:13:14 refused.

fix.title: The fix: retry only what is safe to repeat, give every write a key, and roll platform changes out a few at a time
fix.text: Make it an API standard the template enforces, so every team gets it without asking. Each call is marked safe to repeat or not; the sidecar retries only the safe ones. Reads are safe. A write becomes safe once it carries a key the service checks: the app names the job once, before the first try, from the thing it is about (visit 8841, not this press), and the visit service notes the key as each try arrives, does the work for a new one and refuses one it has seen, sending back the first result. Keep keys at least as long as any repeat could arrive. Set each limit per try from the service's measured slow answer, written next to the setting, rather than one guess for all. And send every platform change to a few services first, with their owners told what changes and what to watch, before the rest.

limits: A key only catches repeats while the service still remembers it: keys forgotten too soon let a late repeat through, and a key made per press instead of per visit misses a second press.
Marking a call safe to repeat is a judgement each team makes; a write wrongly marked safe brings tonight back, so the platform should check that every write marked safe carries a key.
A few-first rollout only catches what those first services actually do: if none of them makes slow writes, version 3 would have looked fine there too.

explain.seniorTake: A platform's defaults are decisions made once for every team, so they deserve the care of a decision made for every team. Retries are not free: each one is a bet that doing the call again is harmless, and that bet is only true for reads and for writes the service can recognise. Put that knowledge in the platform, not in forty heads: mark calls safe or not, give every write a key, refuse keys already seen, and set limits from measured slow answers. Then treat the platform like a product with customers: tell the owners what is changing, send it to a few services first, watch what those services actually do, and widen it only then. Staff work here is reading the other team's default as if it were your own code, because on the night it is.

realWorld.title: Istio: two retries by default
realWorld.text: Istio's Traffic Management page says: "The default retry behavior for HTTP requests is to retry twice before returning the error." Of the gap between tries: "The interval between retries (25ms+) is variable and determined automatically by Istio". Moonmitten's 3 retries were its platform team's own setting.

realWorld.title: Istio: no timeout by default
realWorld.text: The same page: "The Envoy timeout for HTTP requests is disabled in Istio by default." Envoy is the proxy Istio places beside each service, its sidecar, so a limit per try exists only if someone sets one.

realWorld.title: Istio's example: 3 retries, 2 seconds each
realWorld.text: The page's own example reads: "The following example configures a maximum of 3 retries to connect to this service subset after an initial call failure, each with a 2 second timeout." It is an example, not a default, and it says nothing about whether the call is safe to repeat; a platform that copies it copies that silence too.

realWorld.title: Istio: every call through the sidecar
realWorld.text: "All traffic that your mesh services send and receive (data plane traffic) is proxied through Envoy", the page says, which is why one setting in the mesh reaches every call between services.

realWorld.title: CNCF: a platform is a product
realWorld.text: The CNCF Platforms White Paper says: "Platform teams must treat their platforms like products and develop them together with users."

realWorld.title: CNCF: the golden path
realWorld.text: "Such a workflow could be offered with an initial project template and documentation, a bundle often described as a golden path." A golden path spreads good defaults fast, and bad ones just as fast.

realWorld.title: CNCF: rules built into templates
realWorld.text: "The shared platform patterns also allow embedding governance and controls in templates, patterns and capabilities." Marking calls safe to repeat and requiring keys on writes is that kind of control.

asked: What is a service mesh for?
Which calls are safe to retry?
How would you roll out a platform change to 40 services?
interview.answer: A service mesh puts a helper, a sidecar, beside every service and sends all calls between services through it, so routing, finding services, encryption, limits per try and retries are set in one place instead of in every program. That is its power and its risk: one setting reaches every call. On retries, I'd retry only calls that are safe to repeat: reads, and writes the receiving service can recognise because they carry an idempotency key, named once by the caller before the first try and checked by the service as each try arrives. A cut try isn't a failed one; the server may have finished it, so a write without a key must not be retried blindly. Limits per try should come from each service's measured slow answers. To roll a platform change out to 40 services, I'd treat the platform as a product: write down what changes, tell every owner, send it first to a few services whose calls exercise the change, watch the measures that would show harm, such as repeated writes and error rates, then widen it in steps with a way back. I'd tell the story of a pet-sitting agency whose platform added retries for every call on a Tuesday, and a cat's check-in became four that night, cancelling his next three visits.

terms.def: Someone who visits pets in their own homes at night while the owners are away: lets themselves in, feeds and checks the animal, and checks in on the agency's app.
The pet-sitting agency in this story. Its app runs on 40 services built by five teams on a platform kept by a sixth.
The button a sitter presses on arriving at a home. Each press is one write to the visit service.
What the visit service does with a press, in two steps: save a check-in line, then mark the home's earliest visit not yet done as done. It names the home, not the visit.
A small program with one job that other programs call over the network, like one desk in a big office. Moonmitten's app runs on 40.
One program asking another to do something and answer, like passing a note across a desk and waiting for it back.
Moonmitten's service that keeps every booking and saves check-ins. It answers in 0.4 seconds, or 2.5 during the nightly report.
Moonmitten's service that plans sitters' routes. Once a minute, on the minute, it checks every route and texts the sitter any change.
A job that reads the whole day's visits every night from 02:00 to 02:30. While it runs the visit service slows to 2.5 seconds an answer.
The ready-made kit a company's own teams build their services on: the template, the sidecar and their settings, kept by one platform team for all the others.
The full name for a platform built inside a company for its own engineers, so each team needn't build the same plumbing. Moonmitten's is kept by a sixth team.
The team that builds and runs the platform for the other teams. At Moonmitten it is led by Mirjam and sits in head office in another town.
The starting copy every new service is made from, with the sidecar and its settings already in. Change it and every service built from it changes too.
Running a platform like something you sell: the other teams are its customers, their needs shape it, and changes are announced and tried before they spread.
The easy, supported way to build a service on a platform, like a signposted footpath: follow it and the right settings come with you.

A small helper program that runs beside a service and carries its calls: it sends each one on, waits up to a limit, cuts the try and may retry. Like a motorbike's sidecar, it goes everywhere the service goes.
All the sidecars in a system and the settings that steer them, so routing, limits and retries are set in one place for every call. Istio is a widely used one.
How long the sidecar waits for an answer to one try before cutting it: 2 seconds in version 3. A per-try timeout. Cutting stops the waiting, not the work.
Sending the same call again after a try was cut or failed. Version 3 allowed up to 3 retries for every call, reads and writes alike.
One sending of a call by the sidecar. A press with 3 retries can be up to four tries.
The sidecar giving up waiting when the limit per try runs out. The service at the other end never hears of it and may still finish the work.
A call that only looks something up and changes nothing, such as loading a sitter's route. Safe to repeat.
A call that saves or changes something, such as a check-in. Each copy that lands does the work again, unless the service can recognise a repeat.
A call whose second copy changes nothing, so retrying it is harmless: reads, and writes that carry a key the service checks. Also called idempotent.
Short for idempotency key: a name for one job, made once by the caller before the first try and sent with every try, so the service can spot a repeat (The Ticket Number).
Where the visit service notes each key as a try arrives: in progress, then done with its result. A key already on the list is refused.
A numbered release of the platform's template. Version 2 had no limit per try and no retries; version 3, from Tuesday 3 November 2026, had 2 seconds and 3.
A service's diary: one line per event. The visit service stamps each line with the moment the call arrived, not when its save finished.
The engineer whose turn it is to answer problems out of hours. Moonmitten's night line rings them. On 4 November 2026, Eoghan.
A system's knack of carrying on when parts of it fail or calls go missing.
The links that carry messages between machines. Calls between services travel over it and are sometimes lost.
Short for Hypertext Transfer Protocol, the request-and-answer language of the web. Most calls between services, Moonmitten's included, use it.
A widely used open-source service mesh. It places an Envoy proxy beside each service and lets a team set routing, timeouts and retries for every call.
An open-source proxy, a program that passes calls on for others. Istio runs one beside each service as its sidecar.
Short for application programming interface: the set of calls a service accepts and what each one does, like a shop counter's list of what you can ask for.
A rule every service's calls must follow, such as "every write carries a key". A platform can enforce it in the template so no team has to remember.
How a change spreads across services, step by step, from the first to all of them (Canary in the Mine). Version 3 went to all 40 at once.
Sending a platform change to a small group of services, their owners told what changes and what to watch, before the rest. A canary for platforms.
The team responsible for a service: its code, its settings and its problems at night. The visits team owns the visit service.
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation, a non-profit that looks after open-source projects such as Kubernetes and Envoy. Its app delivery group wrote the Platforms White Paper.
A cat whose body can't keep its blood sugar steady and needs insulin, a medicine, at set times. Tobermory's 06:00 visit included it.
The diabetic cat in this story. His four night visits, 02:00 to 08:00, were numbered 8841 to 8844.
The visits team's engineer on call on 4 November 2026. He rang Ciarnait back and read her the visit service's log.
Leads Moonmitten's platform team, in head office in another town. Her team wrote version 3 of the template.
If the register asks you to charge a customer again, check the ticket number first (The Ticket Number). Name each job once, before the first try, and let a repeat of that name do nothing.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, such as A.8.32 on change management.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC8.1 covers how changes are made.

atWork: A platform default applied to writes is a common pattern: a mesh or client library is set to retry every call, and somewhere a write that does something each time it lands meets a slow afternoon. Find your platform's retry and timeout settings, wherever they live: the mesh's configuration (on AWS, often Istio or another mesh on Amazon EKS), an API gateway, or a shared client library. For each, ask which calls they cover, and whether writes are included. List your writes and check each one: does it carry a key the service checks, how long is the key kept, and is that longer than the slowest repeat, including a phone that resends after losing signal? Then look at how platform changes reach services: all at once, or a few first, with owners told and something measured before widening? Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.32 (change management) is where an auditor would look for platform changes being planned, tested and communicated; if it is pursuing SOC 2, criterion CC8.1 covers authorising, testing and approving changes to infrastructure and software. Build these in from the first template rather than at audit time. This case names those standards; it does not teach them.

recall.prompt: Your company's platform team updates the shared template so that every call between services gets a 3-second limit per try and up to 2 more tries. Since then, on the last night of each month, when a billing job runs, a handful of customers find two identical orders. What is probably happening, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: During the billing job the orders service is slower than the limit, so tries are cut, yet each still finishes and creates an order
Creating an order is a write that isn't safe to repeat, so retrying it makes another one
Retry only safe calls, and give every write a key the service checks, refusing a key it has seen

recall.model: The billing job slows the orders service past the 3-second limit, so the sidecar cuts the try and sends it again. But cutting only stops the waiting: the orders service carried on and created the order, then created it again for the retry. Creating an order is a write, and it isn't safe to repeat unless the service can recognise a repeat. I'd change the platform's rule so it retries only calls marked safe, reads by default, and give every write an idempotency key, named once by the caller before the first try; the orders service notes each key as a try arrives and refuses one it has already seen, returning the first result. I'd also set the limit from the service's measured slow answer, and send the template change to a few services first, with their owners told.

recall.prompt: In the sim, as built, switch on "she presses again after an error" and set the visit service's answer during the report to 12 seconds. Which single change keeps Tobermory's other three visits booked?
options: Key check at the visit service: on
Retry rule: only calls marked as harmless twice
recall.why: With the key check on, the first try saves at 02:13:19 and every later try, and the whole second press at 02:13:20, carries key 8841 and is refused: one check-in, nothing cancelled. A 10-second limit still cuts each 12-second try: four check-ins from the first press, four more from the second, three visits cancelled. A 04:00 report moves the doubles to the 04:00 visit, cancelling the 06:00 and 08:00. Retrying only safe calls leaves one try, but the second press saves a second check-in and cancels the 04:00 visit.

recall.prompt: According to Istio's Traffic Management page, what does Istio do by default with an HTTP request between services?
options: Retries it 3 times, each try with a 2-second timeout
Retries it twice before returning the error, and sets no timeout
Never retries it, and times out after 15 seconds
Retries it only when the call is marked harmless to send twice
recall.why: The page says: "The default retry behavior for HTTP requests is to retry twice before returning the error." and "The Envoy timeout for HTTP requests is disabled in Istio by default." Three retries with a 2-second timeout is the page's example, not its default, and Istio's default does not ask whether a call is safe to repeat.

recall.prompt: In an interview you're asked: your platform team needs to change a setting in the template that all 40 of the company's services are built from. How would you roll it out?

keyIdeas.idea: Send it to a few services first, chosen because their calls exercise what the change touches, then widen in steps
Tell every owner what changes and what to watch before it reaches them
Measure the harm the change could cause before widening, with a way back

recall.model: I'd treat the platform as a product with 40 customers. First I'd write down what changes and which calls it touches, and tell the owners of every service, so nobody meets it for the first time at night. Then I'd send it to a few services first, chosen because their calls exercise the change; for a retry setting that means at least one service with slow writes, not only read-heavy ones. I'd measure what could go wrong, such as repeated writes, error rates and slow answers, for long enough to cover the quiet hours too. Only then would I widen it in steps, with a quick way to roll back at each step.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The fix held all through December: writes carry keys, only safe calls are retried, and nothing has been cancelled by a double. In January the platform team changed one more thing to save space: the visit service now forgets each key after 10 minutes instead of 24 hours. It went to photos, search and messages on Tuesday 12 January 2027 and to all 40 on Tuesday 19 January. On Thursday 28 January at 23:41:30 I checked in at a house rabbit's basement flat. The check-in saved, but my phone lost signal before the answer came. The app kept the check-in and sent it again, with the same key, when I found signal on the stairs at 23:58:05. The visit service saved it as new and marked the rabbit's 01:00 visit done. The rota service texted me at 23:59:00: "next visits cancelled: done".
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why didn't the key catch this repeat, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The service had forgotten the key before the repeat arrived; keys must be kept longer than the longest time a repeat can take, including a phone's late resend
The first services to get the change never resend late, so the trial couldn't show the harm; the first group must exercise what the change touches
Watch for repeats getting through: alert on two check-ins with one key or for one visit

coldCase.model: The key worked; the visit service had simply forgotten it. My check-in at 23:41:30 saved and noted its key, but the service dropped the key at 23:51:30, and the phone's resend at 23:58:05 arrived with a name nobody remembered, so it looked new. A key only protects as long as it is kept, so keys must be kept longer than the longest time a repeat can take, and a phone that resends after losing signal can take far more than ten minutes; 24 hours or more is the safer floor. The rollout missed it because the first three services, photos, search and messages, never resend late; a first group must exercise what the change touches, here a write that can come back much later. And I'd add an alert on two check-ins for one visit, so a repeat that gets through is seen that night, not in a text.
